The objection targets the proof of the finite-blocker fact via König's lemma. Let's check: the tree proof constructs a pruned tree; if infinite, König gives infinite branch x_1, x_2, ... with selected sets F_k disjoint from {x_1,...,x_k}. One c ∈ C belongs to infinitely many F_k. The text says "Insert c at its first such occurrence...". The idea: modify the branch — replace the branch by a new branch that at stage of first occurrence of c in F_k chooses c instead. The concern: after inserting c, the subsequent selected sets F_D are determined by choice of F_D disjoint from D; the tree construction says "choose a member F_D disjoint from D" — the choice is arbitrary. The text's argument seems to be a comparison: consider the modified branch where at the node with label D (before selecting x_{k+1}), the set selected is F_{k} (same set as original, containing c). Since F_k is disjoint from D ∪ {c}? Wait original: F_k disjoint from {x_1,...,x_k}, and c ∈ F_k. If we replace x_{k+1} (which was selected from F_k = F_{x_1...x_k}) by c, then new label D' = {x_1,...,x_k, c}. The next selected set F_{k+1} in original is disjoint from {x_1,...,x_{k+1}}. Is it disjoint from D'? We need F_{k+1} not containing c — yes since F_{k+1} ∩ {x_1..x_{k+1}} = ∅ but c might be in F_{k+1} if c wasn't among x_1..x_{k+1}. Hmm, actually the sets along original branch F_1, F_2, ... are all disjoint from the elements selected so far, but could contain c. The text says "until the next occurrence nothing changes" — i.e., for stages between occurrences, the selected sets don't contain c... wait but c belongs to infinitely many F_k; between first occurrence and next occurrence, selected sets are F_j not containing c. Are they still valid after inserting c? F_j disjoint from {x_1,...,x_j} in original; in modified branch the label includes c plus fewer x's. Specifically after inserting c at stage k, modified label is {x_1,...,x_k,c}; original continues with x_{k+1},... So original F_{k+1} disjoint from {x_1,...,x_{k+1}} hence disjoint from {x_1,...,x_k,c}? Not necessarily — F_{k+1} disjoint from {x_1,...,x_{k+1}} but might contain c (if c not among x's). If c ∈ F_{k+1}, then that's the "next occurrence" — and indeed the element selected there (x_{k+2}, from F_{k+1}) is dispensable since c meets F_{k+1}, and c is in the set already. So at that node, the branch has a "contracted node" — meaning the child element x_{k+2} is dispensable given the label includes c. If c ∉ F_{k+1}, then F_{k+1} is disjoint from modified label, and can still be used, selecting x_{k+2}. So the modification works: as long as c not in the selected set, the same sets can be used; when c appears, the next selected element is dispensable, giving a contracted node — contradiction with pruning. The objection claims "no proof that subsequent nodes or selected sets remain the same" — but the text's argument does implicitly show this: if the selected set F contains c, that's an occurrence and we get contraction; otherwise F is disjoint from current label, so the branch continues. The text is terse but the inference is valid. Actually more carefully: on the modified branch, we're free to choose F_D; the original branch's F_j's provide witnesses: each F_j either contains c (giving contraction) or is disjoint from the current modified label, so the branch can continue with the same x's until c occurs. So the argument works. Verdict: rejected. The objection misreads: the "next occurrence" refers to occurrences of c in the original branch's selected sets, and at that node the selected element is dispensable because c (already in the label) meets the selected set. This is a valid argument, if terse.

Is the contraction notion exactly "an earlier chosen element has become dispensable"? Yes: c chosen earlier becomes dispensable? Hmm — dispensable means: D ∪ {x} with x removed still a transversal? "contract a node whenever an earlier chosen element has become dispensable" — at the node where selected set contains c, the child's new element x is dispensable? Actually the text says "the element selected there is dispensable, because that selected set is already met by c". So we can contract: skip adding x. Fine. The proof is compressed but mathematically valid. Reject.
